title: Private Deployments: VPC & On‑Prem Reference, Day‑2 Ops, Upgrade/Rollback, and Customer Requirements
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This document is the canonical reference for Redwood Inference private deployments: VPC-hosted private control plane and inference runtime, and fully on‑prem (air‑gapped) packaging. It combines: deployment checklists, reference architectures, on‑prem packaging requirements, day‑2 operational guidance, and upgrade/rollback procedures. Intended audience: SREs, platform engineers, solutions engineers, and customers running Redwood Private.

Quick links
- Control plane VPC deployment checklist (Section 1)
- Reference architectures (Section 2)
- On‑prem packaging & installer (Section 3)
- Day‑2 operations & runbooks (Section 4)
- Upgrade & rollback playbook (Section 5)
- Customer requirements library (Section 6)

Ownership and support
- Doc owner: eng-private-deployments team (engineering)
- Primary contacts: Aisha Patel (author), Diego Morales (SRE reviewer)
- Support escalation: customer-success -> eng-sre -> eng-platform per escalation-playbook

Summary of artifacts provided
- Terraform modules and example templates for VPC + networking
- Helm charts and Kustomize overlays for Kubernetes deployments
- Air‑gapped installer tarball with dependency manifest and verification scripts
- Day‑2 runbooks (backup, scaling, incident response)
- Upgrade/rollback runbook with prechecks and automated rollback scripts

1) VPC Deployment Guide (control plane + runtime)

Intro
This section covers network topology, IAM, encryption, and common cloud provider specifics for deploying Redwood Private into a customer VPC. The examples below assume AWS; equivalent configs exist for GCP/Azure and are referenced in the repo.

Prerequisites
- Customer provides network ranges (CIDRs) and at least two AZs for redundancy
- DNS zone delegated for control plane (example: redwood-customer.example.com)
- KMS key (customer-managed or provider-managed) for envelope encryption of secrets
- Bastion/jump host or SSM session manager access for initial support

Network requirements (recommended)
- Control plane subnets (private): 10.10.0.0/24 per AZ
- Runtime GPU subnets (private): 10.20.0.0/22 per AZ (size depends on node count)
- Management subnet (for jump hosts): 10.30.0.0/26
- Allowed egress: HTTP/HTTPS to package mirrors (or mirror inside VPC for air‑gapped installs)
- Required ports (inbound to control plane): 443 (API), 2222 (optional support SSH), 5671 (internal message queue, if used)
- Healthcheck path: /internal/health (HTTP 200) on control-plane LB

Security groups and ACLs
- Control plane SG: allow 443 from customer CIDRs and customer ALBs; allow intra-VPC from runtime subnets
- Runtime SG: allow outbound 443 and 9000 (model artifact service), allow inbound from control-plane SG only

IAM and service accounts
- Create dedicated IAM role for Redwood control plane with least privilege: S3 read/write for artifacts, KMS decrypt/encrypt, CloudWatch/Logging write, EC2 describe for autoscaling
- Use IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) for Kubernetes workloads to minimize cluster IAM footprint

Example Terraform snippet (conceptual)
> resource "aws_vpc" "redwood" {
>   cidr_block = "10.10.0.0/16"
>   tags = { Name = "redwood-customer-vpc" }
> }

Deployment verification checklist
1. DNS resolves control-plane domain to ALB IPs (dig/host)
2. TLS certificate is valid and trusted by customer infrastructure
3. /internal/health returns 200 from both control-plane and runtime endpoints
4. KMS decrypt operations succeed from control-plane pods

2) Reference architectures

Overview of models by scale
- Small (proof-of-concept): single-AZ, mixed CPU/GPU nodepool, local PVC object store, single control-plane replica, limited retention metrics 
- Medium (production): multi-AZ control-plane, GPU node pool (2–8 GPUs), dedicated object storage (S3), Prometheus+Grafana, ELK or hosted logging, HA control-plane (3 replicas)
- Enterprise (regulated): private control plane in VPC with dedicated KMS/HSM, private peering to customer network, dedicated logging/archive bucket with retention policies, PCI/PHI controls, SLA-backed Dedicated pools for throughput

Components (standard deployment)
- Control plane: API server, scheduler, config store (Postgres), secrets manager (Vault or KMS integrations)
- Inference runtime: GPU-backed node pool, container runtime with NVIDIA device plugin, model cache (local NVMe), runtime agent for KV cache and batching
- Storage: S3-compatible object store for model artifacts; optional NFS for shared files in air-gapped installs
- Observability: Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, Fluentd/Fluent Bit -> ELK/Cloud logging
- Networking: ALB/NLB in front of control-plane, private peering or Transit Gateway to customer network

Diagrams
- Diagrams are available in the repo (reference-arch-diagrams/*.svg). Each diagram shows AZ-level placement, control-plane replicas, runtime pools, and monitoring pipeline.

3) On‑prem packaging and air‑gapped installer

Packaging options
- Standard: Helm charts + image registry credentials pointing to customer registry
- Air‑gapped: tarball with container images (OCI layout), installer binaries, dependency manifests, and verification script (sha256 checksums)

OS and hardware prerequisites
- Supported OS: Ubuntu 20.04/22.04 LTS, Rocky Linux 8+ (list maintained in repo)
- Kernel: 5.4+ (or vendor supported) with NVIDIA driver compatibility
- Container runtime: containerd 1.6+ with cri plugin, or Docker (deprecated)
- GPU drivers: NVIDIA driver 525.x+ and NVIDIA container toolkit, nvidia-container-runtime/OCI hooks
- Kubernetes: v1.25 – v1.27 (matrix in repo). For air‑gapped we support exactly-tested versions; runbook lists required patches.

Installer workflow (air‑gapped)
1. Verify hardware and OS prereqs using provided preflight.sh
2. Load image bundle: ./installer load-images --bundle /path/to/bundle.tar.gz
3. Apply CRDs and Helm charts offline: ./installer apply --values ./values-airgap.yaml
4. Run post-install verification: ./installer verify --checks health,kms,s3

Example values.yaml excerpt (text)
> global:
>   storageClass: local-nvme
>   runtimeMode: onprem
> nodePools:
>   - name: gpu-pool
>     count: 4
>     instanceType: p4d.24xlarge # example mapping for on-prem: 8xA100 equivalent

4) Day‑2 operations (Monitoring, scaling, runbooks)

SLOs and target thresholds (example)
- API availability (control-plane): 99.95% monthly
- Runtime request latency (p95, cold-start excluded): <= 120ms for small models, variable for large models (documented per model)
- Error budget (control-plane): 0.05% per month -> alert at 50% burn

Monitoring and alerting
- Baseline alerts: control-plane unready, database replication lag > 5s, model fetch failures > 5/min, GPU OOM rate > 1/hour per node
- Cost/Utilization dashboards: per-node GPU utilization, per-model tokens-per-second, batch size distribution

Scaling guidelines
- Autoscaling: use HorizontalPodAutoscaler for control-plane components where appropriate; use Cluster Autoscaler for GPU pools with node group size limits
- Predictable throughput: reserve minimum node counts for peak windows (use reserved capacity in Dedicated offering or equivalent on-prem pool sizing)

Backups and retention
- Postgres WAL: continuous replication with point-in-time recovery; daily snapshots and 7-day WAL retention for production
- Model artifact store: versioned objects with lifecycle rules (retain last N versions per model)
- Key rotation: rotate KMS keys annually or per customer policy

Common runbooks (links)
- Model fetch failures -> runbooks/model-fetch-failure
- GPU OOM -> runbooks/gpu-oom-mitigation
- Control-plane DB failover -> runbooks/db-failover

5) Upgrade and rollback procedures

Principles
- Always run upgrades first in a staging/canary cluster that mirrors production (same Kubernetes version, same node types)
- Keep database migrations reversible where possible; run migrations as separate step and monitor replication

Pre-upgrade checklist
1. Verify backups (Postgres snapshot & object store snapshot) are complete and verified
2. Confirm canary cluster is healthy and has been running the target release for at least 24 hours
3. Ensure no long-running jobs or config changes in flight
4. Announce maintenance window to stakeholders and set increased paging thresholds

Canary rollout steps (example)
1. Create a canary release with 5% traffic routed to new control-plane instances (use ingress weighted routing or proxy rule)
2. Monitor key metrics for 30–60 minutes: error rate, latency, model fetch success, KMS operations
3. If metrics are stable, incrementally increase to 25%, 50%, then full cutover; perform DB migrations only after control-plane is stable at 50%

Rollback procedure (fast rollback)
1. Pause traffic to new instances or revert ingress weight to 0%
2. If DB migrations were run and are irreversible, follow emergency rollback runbook (may require restoring from snapshot and replaying WAL)
3. Validate old release health: run smoke tests for API endpoints and model inference
4. Open postmortem and capture root cause

Automated rollback guardrails
- Automatic rollback triggers: p95 latency increase > 2x baseline, error rate > 1% absolute increase, failed health checks > 3 in 5 minutes

6) Customer requirements library (checklist for onboarding)

Network & connectivity
- Public IPs required: No (private VPC preferred). If needed: ALB with customer-provided certificate
- Outbound egress: allow HTTPS to package mirrors or provide mirror in VPC

Security & compliance
- Data residency: list acceptable regions and buckets for artifact storage
- Encryption: KMS for secrets, TLS for all in‑flight traffic, at‑rest encryption for object store and DB
- Audit logging: enabled and shipped to customer SIEM for regulated customers

Capacity planning
- Expected throughput: tokens/sec or requests/sec per model; typical starter sizes: 2x A100-equivalent GPUs for development, 8–32 GPUs for production medium workloads
- Storage: model artifacts (each large model 5–50GB depending on quantization); plan for N versions and snapshot retention

Operational responsibilities (example table)
- Customer: network provisioning, firewall rules, on‑prem hardware lifecycle, access control to KMS keys (if customer-managed)
- Redwood: control-plane software, runtime images, security patches for provided packages, guided support for upgrades

Checklist (onboarding)
- [ ] Network ranges and peering details provided
- [ ] DNS handed over for control-plane domain
- [ ] KMS key & IAM roles created
- [ ] GPU nodes provisioned and validated (driver tests pass)
- [ ] Backup schedule approved and tested

7) Troubleshooting and runbooks (common issues)

Symptom: long model fetch times
- Check S3 object store latency and throughput
- Verify model cache hit ratio: low cache hit -> warm cache using bulk prefetch
- Inspect network ACLs and MTU mismatches between nodes and storage

Symptom: GPU OOM during inference
- Reduce batch size or enable dynamic batching thresholds
- Check model quantization profile; use quantized variant if acceptable

Symptom: control-plane API 503 errors
- Check control-plane pods for memory/CPU pressure, restart counts
- Confirm DB connectivity and replication lag
